exercises.label: Exercise 5.B1 — Medium: Certify the gain the actuator might implement
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The correct command interval is stated compactly. Explain why interval containment reduces to the two endpoint inequalities, rearrange each, test the actual allowed1.6 realization and distinguish being outside a certified union from proved physical unsafety. Show the inclusive/strict-headroom boundary conventions.
exercises.replacement_html:
Certify the gain actually executed. The previous evidence certifies every gain in $S=[-1,1.55]$. A command $a$ may be realized as $a+\varepsilon$ with $|\varepsilon|\le0.1$, so all possible implementations fill $[a-0.1,a+0.1]$. The command passes only if this entire interval lies in $S$.

Check both extreme realizations. Because both sets are intervals, containment is equivalent to requiring the smallest realization to be no smaller than the certified lower endpoint and the largest to be no larger than its upper endpoint:

$$\begin{aligned} a-0.1\ge-1&\iff a\ge-1+0.1=-0.9,\\ a+0.1\le1.55&\iff a\le1.55-0.1=1.45. \end{aligned}$$

The allowable command interval is therefore $[-0.9,1.45]$.

Test command1.5. Its possible realizations are $[1.4,1.6]$. The upper realization1.6 is outside the certified union, since $1.6\gt1.55$, so command1.5 is not robustly certified. The command's nominal value being inside $S$ does not cover that implementation error. An excluded gain need not actually be unsafe; it has no guarantee from the available cones.

At command1.45 the largest realized gain is exactly1.55, where the second cone's lower headroom is $0.60-0.8|1.55-0.8|=0.60-0.8(0.75)=0$. This is allowed by the non-strict requirement $f\ge0$. The lower endpoint command$-0.9$ likewise permits realization$-1$, at the first cone's zero-margin boundary. To certify strictly positive headroom for every realization using these cones, choose commands strictly inside $(-0.9,1.45)$. The noise, Lipschitz and experiment-execution assumptions remain part of the certificate.

exercises.label: Exercise 5.B2 — Hard: Replace deterministic noise by a finite-run event
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The existing solution correctly handles conditional adaptive noise and the union bound, but compresses the logarithm/reversal/square-root steps into a verbal instruction and gives the final cone radius directly. Show the tower expectation, union-bound budget, every algebraic transformation to E and the observation-based radius, retaining finite-horizon conditional assumptions and the independent safe seed.
exercises.replacement_html:
Keep the assumption valid after adaptive choices. Let $\mathcal F_{i-1}$ be the information used to choose experiment$i$. The question assumes that, conditional on that information, its sensor error is still Gaussian with mean zero and standard deviation$0.15$ degrees. Thus the supplied tail bound gives

$$\Pr(|\epsilon_i|\gt E\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}) \le2\exp\left(-\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}\right).$$

Averaging conditional probabilities over the histories gives the unconditional probability. Since the right-hand side is the same constant for every history,

$$\Pr(|\epsilon_i|\gt E) =\mathbb E\big[\Pr(|\epsilon_i|\gt E\mid\mathcal F_{i-1})\big] \le2\exp\left(-\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}\right).$$

This is why adaptive gain selection does not invalidate the stated bound; a merely unconditional Gaussian description would not automatically supply this conditional premise.

Allocate the envelope-failure budget across the whole run. A union bound over at most100 experiments yields

$$\Pr\big(\text{some }|\epsilon_i|\gt E\big) \le\sum_{i=1}^{100}\Pr(|\epsilon_i|\gt E) \le200\exp\left(-\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}\right).$$

No independence between these failure events is needed. To make their combined probability at most0.01, solve

$$\begin{aligned} 200\exp\left(-\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}\right)&\le0.01\\ \exp\left(-\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}\right)&\le\frac{0.01}{200}=\frac1{20000}\\ -\frac{E^2}{2(0.15)^2}&\le-\ln(20000)\\ E^2&\ge2(0.15)^2\ln(20000). \end{aligned}$$

The logarithm is increasing; multiplying the resulting inequality by a negative number reverses its direction. An envelope radius is nonnegative, so the smallest sufficient choice from this tail bound is

$$E=0.15\sqrt{2\ln(20000)}\approx0.667575\ \text{degrees}.$$

Convert the first observation into a safe cone on that envelope event. When every error is within$E$, the reading$y_0=0.95$ implies $f(0)\ge0.95-E\approx0.282425$ degrees. With Lipschitz constant$L=0.8$ and threshold zero,

$$f(a)\ge0.95-E-0.8|a|\ge0 \quad\text{if}\quad |a|\le r:=\frac{0.95-E}{0.8}\approx0.353031.$$

The domain in this lab is the entire real line, so the first cone certifies$[-r,r]$. The numerator is positive here; a negative numerator would provide no certificate from this observation, though the independently validated seed would remain known safe.

On the simultaneous envelope event, the deterministic cone/previously-safe-query induction applies throughout the planned run. Its failure probability is at most0.01, hence the safe-run guarantee is at least0.99 under the stated seed, fixed-function, Lipschitz and execution assumptions. The smaller radius than the original deterministic radius1 pays for Gaussian tails over100 uses. This finite-horizon bound cannot be extended beyond100 experiments without another justified probability budget or an all-time bound; Gaussian standard deviation alone is never a deterministic error envelope.

exercises.label: Exercise 5.P1 — Easy: Build one LoSBO safety cone
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The opening easy answer gives the right interval but omits the chain from noisy observation to Lipschitz transfer and the domain intersection, and evaluates0.65 without its0.25 distance. Display the lower bound and inequality rearrangement, both distances and endpoints, and clarify that a below-threshold lower certificate is not an actual unsafe value.
exercises.replacement_html:
Remove the possible favorable measurement error. The observation is $y=f(z)+\epsilon$ at $z=0.4$, with $|\epsilon|\le E=0.1$. Therefore $f(z)=y-\epsilon\ge y-E=0.7-0.1=0.6$.

Transfer that lower bound to another point. With Lipschitz constant$L=2$,

$$f(x)\ge f(z)-2|x-z|\ge0.6-2|x-0.4|.$$

To certify the threshold$h=0.2$, require this lower bound to be at least0.2:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.6-2|x-0.4|&\ge0.2\\ 2|x-0.4|&\le0.4\\ |x-0.4|&\le0.2\\ 0.2\le x&\le0.6. \end{aligned}$$

The last step expands the absolute-value inequality. Intersecting$[0.2,0.6]$ with the allowed domain$D=[0,1]$ leaves$[0.2,0.6]$ unchanged.

Check the proposed points. At$x=0.6$, the distance is$|0.6-0.4|=0.2$, so the lower bound is$0.6-2(0.2)=0.6-0.4=0.2$. Equality meets the non-strict threshold, so this point is certified. At$x=0.65$, the distance is$0.25$, so the lower bound is$0.6-2(0.25)=0.6-0.5=0.1$, below0.2. This observation does not certify that point; it does not prove its actual value is0.1 or that it is unsafe.

This is the region certified by the new observation. Earlier valid safe witnesses remain available in the accumulated safe set, even when their points lie outside this one cone. The argument depends on the stated noise bound and Lipschitz constant being valid on the domain.
